court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A bathing-house keeper who let upper-floor rooms to lodgers was not liable for a lodger's loss of property by theft, since a lodging-house keeper does not take a lodger's goods into custody as a bailee, and here the lodger's own failure to lock his door defeated any claim of negligence.

quotes.text: The defendant kept a bathing-house, the upper floors of which were let in apartments to lodgers.
There is authority for holding that a lodging-house keeper, like the defendant, does not assume responsibility for the goods of his lodger, as he does not take them into his custody

notes: Foreclosure-receiver dispute over apartment rental surplus; procedural receivership question, not the character or regulation of short-term letting.

holding_summary: A householder who let her own furnished house at a monthly rent, with an added monthly charge when she was absent and not furnishing board, could maintain statutory summary proceedings against the occupant for nonpayment of the added sum; the hiring was an entire, non-apportionable contract, and inclusion of furniture in the demise did not defeat the ordinary landlord-tenant summary remedy.

quotes.text: Summary proceedings to dispossess a tenant may be maintained under the statute, against the occupant of a furnished house.

Mrs. Iris C. Swigley let the furnished house, No. 41 West Forty-fifth street, to J. Alfred Jones, from August 1, 1878, till May 1, 1879, at $150 per month, with the further proviso that if Mrs. Swigley was absent from and did not receive board upon the premises she was to be entitled to the further sum of $25 per month.
Judge McAdam overruled this objection, holding that the contract was entire, and must be performed in its entirety ; that the lease called for a fixed rent, and that it could not be apportioned

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Where a party expressly contracted for boarding-house rooms with board for a fixed term at a weekly rate, an early departure prompted by medical advice that a change of scene might benefit a family member's health did not excuse further payment, and the boarding-house keeper recovered the full contract price, since only impossibility by law or act of God -- not a disappointed hope of benefit that could have been contracted against -- excuses performance.

quotes.text: The plaintiff testified that there was an express contract to engage the rooms from November 1 to June 1, following, at $70 a week
Boarding-house keepers have the same lien upon baggage and effects of a boarder, for the amount due, as an innkeeper (L. 1860, p. 771, c. 446).
The act only applies to those who make a business, in whole or in part, of keeping boarders (Cody v. McDowell, 1 Lans. 484).
